Into the Light - assisting drug users

By: Jacqui Jayamaha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
"Current Drug rehabilitation methods are failing dismally, indicating that in South Africa - we are certainly not winning the war on drugs – in fact we are just driving it further underground.

Unique Selling Point:
The first low threshold Opioid Substitution Therapy Project (OST) in South Africa has recently opened up in Durban. Unlike most rehabilitation facilities, heroin users are met where they are at, with recognition that they have human rights and that drug use is a public health issue, not a criminal one.


Summary:
Currently in South Africa – According to the Medical Research Council - the success rate for heroin rehabilitation methods, across the board, at private and government provincial centers, is only + - 7%, leaving us with a daunting + - 93% failure rate.Hundreds of thousands of rand is spent by users and institutions annually, on ineffective treatment intervention methods, regardless of their “sophisticated” approaches.The first low threshold Opioid Substitution Therapy Project (OST) in South Africa has recently opened up in Durban. Unlike most rehabilitation facilities, heroin users are met where they are at, with recognition that they have human rights and that drug use is a public health issue, not a criminal one.

The results are astounding. For the first time people who use drugs, who have joined this project feel that they can talk openly about their drug use habits, and receive assistance from a team that neither judges them nor has unrealistic expectations of abstinence. Equally importantly, the Durban OST Project provides heroin users with medical assistance (with carefully observed Methadone provision), which makes ‘detoxification’ less daunting, and provides hope for maintaining a life that they define as normal and healthy.

Out patient programme - The fact that this is an outpatient programme is important. Beneficiaries are not taken away from their everyday environment and hidden from sight. Instead, the team at the Durban OST Project works together with support persons that are seen as invaluable to the success of normalisation of life for people with heroin use disorders.



Further information:
A ground breaking approach never seen before in South Africa - Why is this approach different from most other drug rehabilitation facilities? Most importantly, this project has a ‘harm reduction approach’, which means that instead of prohibiting drugs and criminalizing drug users, what is aimed for, is interventions that reduce the harms of drugs and drug conventional policy. People who use drugs are understood as having undergone experiences that either gave rise to feelings of disconnect or resulted from trauma. What is required then is not criminalization and further punishment, but support. In order to give optimal support, and to work in the light, the project advocates for decriminalisation of drug possession and drug use.

Menelisi Ngidi Ex heroine user
"Timothy" "venter" Timothy is newly recruited on the programme
"Jane" "Brown" Jane has been a heroine user for a long time and is new on the OST programme. She is Timothy's partner.
Zama Mdlalose Zama is Menelisi's partner and pregnant with his child. He is the support system for Menilisi's recovery
Pierre Oberholzer Ex user on the OST project beneficiary ex heroin user

Expert:
Prof. Monique Marks Prof. Marks heads up the OST programme and is in close contact with beneficiaries and staff members of the centre.
Dr. Terence Moodley Medical Practitioner at the Clinic

Locations:
Umbilo, Berea and Mt Edgecombe in Kwazulu Natal

Press Release:


Opioid Substitution Therapy
Heroin is one of the most addictive drugs in the world and millions of addicts are simply unable to
overcome the addiction. In South Africa, heroin rehabilitation methods have proven to be a massive failure
and up to 93% of addicts relapse. Now a pilot project in Kwa-Zulu-Natal, called Opioid Substitution
Therapy, could give users and their families new hope.

Script:


Script final “Into the Light” 8 mins Carte Blanche - October 2017

V/O “15% of our country’s population is suffering with a drug problem. (Crowds in town)
After marijuana, Heroin is the leading drug of choice. Known as the King of drugs it is considered one of the most dangerous and addictive narcotics in the world. (Pics guys smoking, shooting, under blanket lying down)
Devi Link “Addiction cuts through all sectors of society – no economic or social background is exempt”.
Interview (Notha Nesta) Inside I feel like I’m alone on the earth - no one likes me, get along with me. Like I’m being thrown in the bush, it’s very sad, painful
V/O “Notha Nesta was abused by both his parents and ran away from home at age 13. He has been living on the streets since. (B roll Notha coming down over the wall onto garbage and out onto pavement)
01:23 (Notha Nesta) I lived with my stepmother and we not getting along at all, and my father also don’t care with me a lot. (B roll Nesta standing by wall)
01:41 - And they used to chase me away from home” (b roll standing against wall)
V/O “Nesta began using heroin to deal with the abandonment he felt”.
14:06 (Notha Nesta) – I can’t keep up without a shot a day, sometimes if I don’t have money, if I’m trying it’s like I can kill myself, it’s like I can say God right take me, there’s no use, there’s nothing I’m living for.
V/O The drug reaches the brain fastest when it is injected directly into the bloodstream. (Vis smoking and injecting)
15:19 (Notha Nesta) Ah…oh I’m feeling very comfortable, I’m feeling very cool…………..it tastes nice, I’m feel like there’s nice things running in my veins, my blood, (sucks in breath)……..ya the stress for the day it’s klaar. I don’t have any problem now. (Notha Injecting and telling how he feels)
V/O Psychiatrist, Dr Hemant Nowbath is a substance abuse expert. (Devi and Hemant walking in)
Interview (Hemant Nowbath) Addiction is often seen as a self-inflicted trouble, and people that think that way don’t recognise neuro biological basis of addiction.
Devi noddy
Interview (Hemant Nowbath) The initial decision to use a drug is obviously voluntary, people start experimenting with it, then it moves on to recreational use, misuse and finally addiction. Now in that process a whole lot of changes take place in the brain and that’s what drives the process and that’s why it’s a medical problem that needs proper treatment.
V/O Heroin releases dopamine - the pleasure transmitter, up to 10 times the amount naturally produced by the brain. (new shutterstock footage of dopamine flooding the brain)
Extended use of the drug increases tolerance forcing the person to use larger amounts to reach the same high and withdrawal symptoms like stomach cramps, nausea and vomiting become more severe. (Man lying under blanket – last shoot)
Devi “Heroin addiction is a massive problem in South Africa”.
00:22:37:14 (Hemant Nowbath) If you look at our situation in the country today, 14 million people go to bed hungry every night, unemployment sits at about 35%, we have people living in absolute poverty, so we create conditions that drive people to be prone to develop a whole range of mental illnesses, addiction problems, and then we don’t offer treatment. We then criminalise the problem, and that’s the issue. (B – roll
V/O “Depression and a sense of social isolation are some of the major factors driving heroin use”.
Devi Link “Desperate family and users spend millions of rands on heroin rehabilitation every single year, but with an alarming relapse rate of over 90%. Are we winning the war?”
Interview 18:13:38:05 (Prof. Marks) The war on drugs is an absolute disaster in South Africa, we are simply having a prison population increasing of people who should be getting help and we having a police force operating, doing things that are wasting their time and not assisting with the real problems that we have in South Africa and we are not winning because the people that have a problematic drug use issue are not getting the help that they need.
V/O That help, according to Sociologist Professor Monique Marks, comes in the form of a groundbreaking rehabilitation treatment, Opioid Substitution Therapy or OST. Launched in Kwazulu Natal, this privately funded pilot project, is medically supervising, methadone substitution for 50 heroin users for 18 months. (Monique at desk. OST)

V/O “Methadone is dispensed to volunteer beneficiaries to replace the noxious drug. Although it is an opioid like heroin, methadone is slow releasing and attaches to the receptors in the brain for up to 36 hours – whereas the effects of heroin only last between 4 – 6 hours. Blocking cravings and withdrawals, it gives users a good chance to abstain from heroin till recovery, without irreversible damage to vital organs and the brain. (Use above to replace VO below if possible)
(It blocks the cravings and reduces the withdrawals and does not present the same irreversible damage to vital organs and deterioration of the brain).
Interview (Hemant Nowbath) “The programme’s a holistic programme, its designed to get patients off the streets, its designed to get their medication as opposed to getting illicit drugs from a drug dealer”
Devi “And has it been successful?”
Interview (Hemant Nowbath) “Absolutely, talk to the people who have been going through the programme”.
Interview (Sharon Malgas) 15:24:07:09 “My son has had a problem since the age of 13 with drugs, we’ve tried numerous rehabs, he hasn’t lasted long they haven’t been of any help to him. I’ve seen a vast change in him since he joined the OST programme. He seems more able to cope with what goes on around him.
V/O “Sharon is optimistic about her son’s recovery since he joined the OST programme..
Interview (Sharon Malgas) It’s been 5 months now and I honestly see a tremendous change in my son.
V/O Beneficiaries are treated as out patients, report to the Clinic daily, receive their methadone dose and are monitored regularly by a physician. Treatment includes psychosocial consultation and group therapy.
V/O ”Menelisi Ngidi was one of OST’s first beneficiaries - he dropped out of University when he started using heroin. (B roll Menelisi walking down the Road)
Menelisi 17:01:10:09 “I had already tried to stop many times, it’s not that. I have always wanted to stop – but every time I’d stop there’d be something that would bring me back to it there is always this trigger.”
Devi “ What has the OST programme done for you?”
Menelisi” I am taking this methadone and I have a choice not to take heroin, you see, I have that choice”.
V/O Now working as a car guard, Menelisi is determined to go back to University and finish his degree. (Car guarding end on thumbs up)
V/O “In many countries, for example in the Netherlands, the programme has been hailed a great success where heroin use under the age of 40 is practically non-existent and 80% of OST patients have found employment. Professor Marks is frustrated at the lack of South African government funding”
Interview Prof. Marks “OST has been running internationally for the last 30 years – we are far, far behind.
Devi “ But why are we so way behind the rest of the world?”
Interview (Prof Marks) We knew that ARV’s worked but we had to prove it, we to advocate for it, we needed TAC, we needed people to die, we need a whole lot of things before we could get ARV’s online and available. This, its a similar kind of process that we are going through with Opioid substitution therapy.
Interview (Hemant Nowbath) “The World Health Organisation says that Methadone should be part of an essential drugs list. Here we don’t have these drugs readily available in our state facilities, and for me the fact that we don’t have them available becomes a human rights issue”.
Devi Link “Something’s got to give, our current methods and attitudes are not taking us any closer to a solution. We keep talking about this war on drugs, but from where I’m standing, nobody’s winning”.
Interview (Menelisi) “A person who’s like a drug addict – I promise you most of them, most of them don’t want to be where they are. I promise you”.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Promo 1
V/O “ Recently introduced into South Africa, an innovative, heroin drug rehabilitation programme is bringing renewed hope to families and users”

Promo 2
V/O "15 % of South African’s have a drug problem, statistics show that current rehabilitation methods have a relapse rate of up to 90% - can the newly launched Opioid Substitution Therapy be the solution?”

Promo 3
Up sound Interview (Prof. Marks) "The war on drugs is an absolute disaster in South Africa",
V/O Professor Marks is driving a rehabilitation project – OST, that is offering a substitute for heroin.

Promo 4
Devi to camera
"Recently introduced into South Africa, an innovative, heroin drug rehabilitation programme is bringing renewed hope to families and users”
